issue: Does 28 U.S.C. § 1355(b) confer in rem jurisdiction over forfeiture of foreign property without actual or constructive control over the res, or does due process require such control?

sides.position: Section 1355(b) alone confers in rem jurisdiction on the district where the act or omission giving rise to forfeiture occurred; actual or constructive control of the res is not required.
cases: United States v. Certain Funds Located at the Hong Kong & Shanghai Banking Corp., 96 F.3d 20 (D.C. Cir. 1996)
Contents of Account No. 03001288 v. United States, 344 F.3d 399 (3d Cir. 2003)
United States v. Approximately $1.67 Million (US) in Cash, Stock, and Other Valuable Assets Held by or at: (1) Total Aviation Ltd., 513 F.3d 991 (9th Cir. 2008)

sides.position: Constructive control of the res is required for in rem jurisdiction, and the statute must be read consistently with that due process requirement.
cases: United States v. Meza, 63 F.3d 148 (2d Cir. 1995)
United States v. Nasri, No. 22-55685 (9th Cir. 2026)

this_court: does not decide clearly from the excerpts; the dissent reads the majority as aligning with the Second Circuit's Meza control requirement, while the dissent takes the D.C. and Third Circuit position
quote: On my read, there remains a circuit split on the meaning of § 1355.
cite: United States v. Younes Nasri, No. 22-55685 (9th Cir. 2026)
